reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine
clinicalPearls: Caused by mutations in COL7A1, which encodes type VII collagen, the main component of the anchoring fibrils that secure the epidermis to the dermis
Blistering occurs below the lamina densa (sublamina densa) in the superficial dermis, so healing characteristically produces scarring and milia
It occurs in dominant (usually milder) and recessive (often severe) forms, with the severe generalised recessive type causing the most disabling disease
Repeated blistering and scarring of the hands and feet leads to fusion of the digits and a mitten (pseudosyndactyly) deformity in severe recessive disease
Mucosal involvement causes oesophageal strictures, dysphagia, and malnutrition, and dental and ocular complications are common
Chronic non-healing wounds in severe recessive disease carry a high risk of aggressive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, a leading cause of death in adulthood
Management is multidisciplinary and supportive, with meticulous wound care, nutritional support, contracture prevention, and vigilant skin cancer surveillance
reference.pathophysiology: Type VII collagen, encoded by COL7A1, forms the anchoring fibrils that tether the lamina densa of the basement membrane to the underlying papillary dermis. In dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, mutations reduce or abolish functional type VII collagen so anchoring fibrils are deficient or absent, and the skin separates beneath the lamina densa in the superficial dermis in response to minor trauma. Because the split lies within the dermis, repair occurs with fibrosis, producing scarring, milia, and progressive contractures rather than clean healing. Dominant mutations typically retain more residual collagen function and cause milder disease, whereas recessive loss-of-function mutations produce severe generalised disease with extensive scarring, mucosal strictures, and the chronic wounds that predispose to squamous cell carcinoma.
additionalDifferentials: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (autoimmune, also targeting type VII collagen)
Porphyria cutanea tarda and other blistering photodermatoses
Bullous pemphigoid and other autoimmune blistering diseases
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence antigen mapping localising the split below the lamina densa
Transmission electron microscopy assessing anchoring fibrils
Nutritional assessment with monitoring for anaemia and micronutrient deficiency
Contrast swallow or endoscopy to evaluate oesophageal strictures
Regular skin surveillance and biopsy of suspicious non-healing lesions for squamous cell carcinoma
redFlags: A new, enlarging, or non-healing indurated lesion suspicious for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
Progressive dysphagia and weight loss from oesophageal strictures
Severe anaemia and failure to thrive from chronic wounds and poor intake
Progressive pseudosyndactyly and contractures impairing function
reference.prognosis: The dominant forms are generally compatible with a near-normal life expectancy, whereas severe generalised recessive disease is disabling, with progressive contractures, strictures, and a markedly increased risk of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma that is the leading cause of premature death.
pitfalls: Failing to institute skin cancer surveillance in severe recessive disease
Overlooking oesophageal strictures as a cause of malnutrition
Not preventing hand and foot contractures and pseudosyndactyly with early therapy and dressings
Confusing dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa with the autoimmune condition epidermolysis bullosa acquisita
Underestimating the multidisciplinary nutritional, dental, and psychological support required
management: Provide meticulous wound care with atraumatic non-adherent dressings, blister lancing and infection control to protect the fragile sub-lamina-densa skin
Adopt skin-protective handling and trauma avoidance to minimise new blistering
Support nutrition with dietitian input, correcting anaemia and micronutrient deficiency arising from chronic wounds and poor intake
Manage oesophageal strictures with dilatation and a soft diet, and provide regular dental and ocular surveillance and care
Undertake regular skin surveillance with biopsy of suspicious non-healing lesions for aggressive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
Control pain and itch and manage pseudosyndactyly and contractures with physiotherapy and hand surgery
Coordinate care within a specialist epidermolysis bullosa multidisciplinary team and consider emerging gene- and cell-directed therapies
Offer genetic counselling and family testing given COL7A1 inheritance
